questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 18 non-recursive CTE is a SELECT with no volatile functions and is referenced once. What is the default optimization behavior?

sources.title: PostgreSQL: WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)
sources.claim: A side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE referenced once is folded by default. CTE syntax alone does not require a temporary table, an optimization fence or duplicate execution.

questions.explanation: A side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE referenced once is folded by default. CTE syntax alone does not require a temporary table, an optimization fence or duplicate execution.

choices.text: It can be folded into the parent query for joint optimization.
It must be stored in a temporary table before the parent query starts.
It must be evaluated independently because every CTE is an optimization fence.
It is always run twice so PostgreSQL can compare the resulting row sets.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 18 `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE` finds a conflicting row, but the update WHERE condition is false. What does `RETURNING` include for that row?

sources.title: PostgreSQL: INSERT
sources.claim: RETURNING includes rows actually inserted or updated. A conflicting row locked but not updated by the condition is omitted, not returned as an existing, proposed or NULL placeholder row.

questions.explanation: RETURNING includes rows actually inserted or updated. A conflicting row locked but not updated by the condition is omitted, not returned as an existing, proposed or NULL placeholder row.

choices.text: The existing row, because every conflicting row is automatically returned.
No row: the conflict row was locked but not updated.
The proposed insertion row, because RETURNING ignores the update condition.
A row of NULL values, because filtering conflicts creates a placeholder.

questions.prompt: You choose a PostgreSQL 18 GIN operator class for a `jsonb` column. Which capabilities are documented? Select all that apply.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: JSON Types
sources.claim: B and E: path_ops supports containment and the jsonpath match operators. A is false because the default operator class supports key existence. C is false because path_ops omits key-exists support. D is false because the operator must apply to an indexed expression.

questions.explanation: B and E: path_ops supports containment and the jsonpath match operators. A is false because the default operator class supports key existence. C is false because path_ops omits key-exists support. D is false because the operator must apply to an indexed expression.

choices.text: Default `jsonb_ops` omits GIN support for the key-exists operator `?`.
`jsonb_path_ops` supports containment with `@>`.
`jsonb_path_ops` supports every key-exists operator supported by `jsonb_ops`.
A GIN index automatically indexes any nested expression in any query shape.
`jsonb_path_ops` supports jsonpath match operators `@?` and `@@`.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 18 side-effect-free CTE is referenced twice. Why might `NOT MATERIALIZED` improve performance?

sources.title: PostgreSQL: WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)
sources.claim: NOT MATERIALIZED permits folding, which can push restrictions into each use but duplicate calculations. It does not guarantee one calculation, write a disk cache or bypass predicates.

questions.explanation: NOT MATERIALIZED permits folding, which can push restrictions into each use but duplicate calculations. It does not guarantee one calculation, write a disk cache or bypass predicates.

choices.text: It guarantees one calculation while forcing every reference to scan all rows.
It permits joint optimization, at the risk of duplicate computation.
It writes the CTE to disk so the parent query can skip all index maintenance.
It bypasses SQL predicates so both references receive the same cached results.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL 18 `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id` encounters an existing key. How should the caller interpret an empty result?

sources.title: PostgreSQL: INSERT
sources.claim: DO NOTHING inserts nothing on that conflict, so RETURNING has no inserted row. It neither deletes the existing row nor implicitly returns its id.

questions.explanation: DO NOTHING inserts nothing on that conflict, so RETURNING has no inserted row. It neither deletes the existing row nor implicitly returns its id.

choices.text: The existing key cannot be present because RETURNING would always show it.
The database deleted the conflicting row before evaluating RETURNING.
That statement inserted no row to return.
The existing id was returned implicitly as an out-of-band result value.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 18 application mainly tests JSON containment and occasionally tests top-level key existence. Which index-design claims are correct? Select all that apply.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: JSON Types
sources.claim: A and B follow the documented operator coverage. D: path_ops indexes path/value combinations and often yields smaller, more specific containment searches. C is false because entries differ; E is false because key-exists is unsupported by path_ops.

questions.explanation: A and B follow the documented operator coverage. D: path_ops indexes path/value combinations and often yields smaller, more specific containment searches. C is false because entries differ; E is false because key-exists is unsupported by path_ops.

choices.text: Switching to `jsonb_path_ops` removes GIN support for key-exists operators.
The default `jsonb_ops` can support both containment and key-exists queries.
Both operator classes produce identical entries for every JSON document.
`jsonb_path_ops` can be more specific and smaller for containment workloads.
A `jsonb_path_ops` index makes every key-exists query use that index automatically.
